schools.summary: Gill reads the date as the third year of Hoshea's revolt from Assyria and works through the arithmetic that makes Ahaz a father at eleven.
Keil and Delitzsch set the whole reign in its arc from Assyrian dependence to the destruction of Sennacherib's army; Ellicott finds the king's name significant and suspects a slip in his mother's.
Henry makes the reign a case of grace against inheritance, and finds providence in the timing of Hezekiah's birth.
Clarke maps the chapter and defers the chronology to an earlier note; Wesley resolves the ages by dating the sixteen years from Ahaz's sole reign.

debates.question: How can Ahaz have been father to a son of twenty-five at his own death?

sides.position: Grotius eases it a year, and the historian's habit of dropping incomplete regnal years leaves nearly fourteen between them
The sixteen years of Ahaz are reckoned not from his accession but from the beginning of his reigning alone

outliers.note: He alone asks why a king so bad produced a king so good, and answers that whatever good there is in any man is not of nature but of grace.

themes: the arithmetic of the two reigns
the meaning of the two names
1.pericope_label: Hezekiah began to reign; twenty and nine years in Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill observes that removing the high places is what the best kings of Judah had never attempted, noted of them to their discredit.
Henry sorts the objects by origin, defends breaking what a father had set up, and reads the serpent as the hardest case because it had divine warrant.
Clarke supplies the cleansing of the temple and the deferred passover, and will not let the name of the serpent be translated; Wesley limits the removal to the high places most frequented.
Ellicott reads the emphatic construction, corrects images to pillars and the groves to a plural, and defends the serpent's Mosaic antiquity.

debates.question: What does the name given to the brasen serpent mean?

sides.position: A term of contempt meaning no more than a brazen serpent, as Jarchi takes it, the Targum making it the people's name rather than the king's
Possibly great serpent rather than brass-god, with the derivation from brass only a popular etymology
Nothing but a piece of brass, which is the point Hezekiah was making

outliers.note: He alone explains the symbol rather than the idolatry, since in Egypt the serpent stood for the healing power of Deity and Moses taught by means suited to the people's capacity.

themes: according to all that David did
3.pericope_label: He removed the high places and brake in pieces the brasen serpent

schools.summary: Gill makes the Targum's Word of the Lord the object of the trust, and the cleaving a cleaving to worship and the fear of the Lord.
Henry makes perseverance the thing Hezekiah was a nonesuch for, and notes the courage abolishing idolatry took.
Clarke numbers the character in four points and its result in two; Wesley defines the trust by what it refused, foreign succours of the kind Ahaz and Asa had sought.
Ellicott contrasts him with kings who trusted the Nehushtan and separates feeling from practice; Keil and Delitzsch refer the verdict to his confidence in God.

debates.question: How can none be like him if the same is said of Josiah?

sides.position: One was pre-eminent in trust, the other in strict adherence to the Mosaic law, so there is no contradiction
Each excelled the other in several respects, Hezekiah's advantage being that he began at once and removed what none durst touch

outliers.note: He alone limits the comparison to the kings of Judah, since David and Solomon were kings of all Israel.

themes: none like him among the kings
5.pericope_label: He trusted in the LORD God of Israel, and clave to him

schools.summary: Gill reads the help through the Targum and makes the Philistine campaign a recovery of towns lost under Ahaz.
Henry ties presence to prosperity, defends the revolt as the assertion of rights Ahaz could not alienate, and draws the parallel between purging corruptions and recovering possessions.
Clarke takes the watchtower phrase for a proverb covering every kind of fortification; Wesley argues at length that the revolt was no sin.
Ellicott warns that these verses are a preliminary sketch and not a chronology; Keil and Delitzsch date the refusal of tribute and explain why Sennacherib came.

debates.question: Was the revolt against Assyria a sin?

sides.position: No: it differs from Zedekiah's case in oath, in covenant and in divine command, and God owned and assisted him in it
No: it is called rebellion only because Assyria called it so, being an assertion of rights Ahaz could not alienate

outliers.note: He alone argues the ethics of revolt by comparing Zedekiah, and rests the verdict on God's never having reproved Hezekiah for it.

themes: from the watchtower to the fenced city
7.pericope_label: The LORD was with him; he smote the Philistines unto Gaza

schools.summary: Gill reads the three years inclusively, so that the end of them means their beginning.
Henry gives three reasons why the fall of Samaria belongs in Hezekiah's reign, and notices the order of hearing and doing in the verdict.
Clarke notes only that the history has been given before.
Ellicott defends the plural verb against the versions and corrects two small points of grammar; Keil and Delitzsch trace the repetition to a second set of annals.

debates.question: Who took Samaria, and does the verb say?

sides.position: The Assyrians, plural, since it was Sargon and not Shalmaneser who took the city
He took it, as the older versions read
holders: the older versions, as reported by Charles Ellicott

outliers.note: He alone explains the repetition by its effect on Judah, the neighbour's house on fire making it time to cast away the accursed thing.

themes: why the story is told twice
Halah, Habor and the cities of the Medes
9.pericope_label: Samaria taken, because they obeyed not the voice of the LORD

schools.summary: Gill dates the invasion relatively and traces Hezekiah's change of mind from defence to purchase, calling it weakness and distrust.
Henry measures the loss of territory, asks where Hezekiah's courage was, and alone defends the stripping of the temple.

Ellicott refuses to smooth the thirteen-year divergence between the Hebrew date and the Assyrian monuments, and reconciles the two tribute figures by the talent used; Keil and Delitzsch record the defensive works and the march to Lachish.
Wesley reads the claim about all the cities as a loose universal and finds three divine purposes in the invader's success.

debates.question: Which date for the invasion is to be trusted?

sides.position: The Assyrian monuments, which are strictly contemporary, against books compiled long after and copied many times
The divergence is remarkable and must not be explained away

outliers.note: He alone justifies taking the gold from the temple doors, by David's precedent with the showbread and by the difference between borrowing a part and plundering in contempt.

themes: the fourteenth year and the monuments
13.pericope_label: Sennacherib came up; Hezekiah sent to Lachish, I have offended

schools.summary: Gill states the plain fact that the tribute was taken and the army sent anyway.
Henry refuses the invader the title of great king and calls the refusal of a personal parley prudence.
Clarke takes the three names for offices after Calmet and supplies a campaign history for the detachment; Wesley reads the breach of faith as justifying the revolt after the event.
Ellicott corrects two of the three titles from the Assyrian and sorts out which pool is meant; Keil and Delitzsch explain the choice of commissioners.

debates.question: What do the three titles mean?

sides.position: Keeper of the tribute, chief of the eunuchs, and master of the wine cellar
Commander-in-chief and chief officer, the Hebrew imitating Assyrian titles, with the second unidentified

outliers.note: He alone reconstructs the strategic situation, with the siege of Lachish raised and an Ethiopian invasion drawing the king home, and judges manifestoes of this kind to have seldom been honourable to their senders.

themes: the conduit of the upper pool
17.pericope_label: Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh come up to Jerusalem

schools.summary: Henry reads the title as the speaker's own idolatry and answers the taunt from the facts of Hezekiah's preparations.
Clarke takes the noun for a diminutive expressing the utmost contempt for Hezekiah's God; Wesley asks what the greatest of men are when God comes to contend with them.
Ellicott supplies a specimen of Assyrian royal style and two guesses at why this officer spoke; Keil and Delitzsch explain the vassal basis of the title and gloss the lip-word.

debates.question: Why did this officer rather than the commander deliver the speech?

sides.position: He may have known Hebrew better than his companions
holders: Thenius, as reported by Charles Ellicott

sides.position: It would have been beneath the commander's dignity, and such language would sound strange in a eunuch's mouth
holders: Schrader, as reported by Charles Ellicott

outliers.note: He alone presses the diminutive form of the noun, so that the question means what little, foolish, unavailing confidence is this.

19.pericope_label: What confidence is this wherein thou trustest? Egypt a bruised reed

schools.summary: Henry answers that the speaker measures the God of Israel by the gods of the heathen, so that the best deed of the reign is read as profanity.
Clarke calls the charge artfully malicious and separates the three things insinuated; Wesley says the man speaks boldly of what he does not understand.

Ellicott canvasses the renderings of the wager and weighs the singular against the plural address; Keil and Delitzsch credit the skill of the move and make the taunt about riders rather than soldiers.

debates.question: Is the sentence addressed to Hezekiah or to his ministers?

sides.position: To Hezekiah, since the versions and the parallel have the singular, which is probably original
To the ministers, keeping the plural, since what follows addresses Hezekiah directly
holders: Thenius and Knobel, as reported by Keil and Delitzsch

outliers.note: He alone names the fallacy, that a God who delighted in many altars is being assumed, so that confining a people to one is taken for an offence.

themes: measuring God by the gods of the heathen
22.pericope_label: Thou sayest, We trust in the LORD; give pledges to my master

schools.summary: Henry denies the speaker any sincerity in the claimed commission and traces what colour it had to reports of God's hand on the ten tribes.
Clarke explains the purpose, to persuade the people that Jehovah had become Assyria's ally; Wesley says the oracle was simply forged to strike terror.

Ellicott repunctuates the verse, identifies the governor as the speaker himself, and collects parallels for invaders claiming the gods of the invaded; Keil and Delitzsch think a report of the prophets was turned to his own purposes.

debates.question: Where did the claim of a divine commission come from?

sides.position: From captive priests of the northern kingdom whom the king had consulted
holders: Michaelis, as reported by Charles Ellicott

sides.position: From reports of the Hebrew prophets, who had called the invasion a judgment
From nothing but the success of the expedition so far
holders: Thenius, as reported by Charles Ellicott

outliers.note: He alone shows the boast to be a convention, producing a Babylonian parallel in which a conqueror claims the favour of the city's own chief god, and the Moabite Stone's oracle to Mesha.

themes: am I come up without the LORD
invaders and the gods of the invaded
a boast truer than he knew
24.pericope_label: Am I now come up without the LORD against this place?

schools.summary: Henry calls the request reasonable by the custom of treaties and the refusal a breach of every rule of decency and honour.
Clarke twice states the purpose, to stir the people to sedition and to make them revolt from their allegiance; Wesley summarises the threat as telling them what miseries he would force on them.

Ellicott identifies Aramaic as the diplomatic language of western Asia and is careful about the name given to Hebrew here; Keil and Delitzsch explain who understood which language, and are precise about the verb for taking up a position.

debates.question: Why did the ministers ask for Aramaean?

sides.position: Because the boasting might make an impression on the people on the wall
Because many of them had worshipped at the high places and might believe Jehovah was incensed at their removal
Because the custom of treaties is that plenipotentiaries settle matters before anything is made public

outliers.note: They alone note that the Masoretes replaced both of the coarse words with euphemisms.

themes: taking a position before the wall
26.pericope_label: Speak in the Syrian language; Rabshakeh cried in the Jews' language

schools.summary: Henry exposes the effrontery of proposing an agreement bought with a present and takes apart both of the advantages held out.
Clarke reads the promise as calculated sedition; Wesley paraphrases the terms as they would have sounded to the hearers.

Ellicott reports the unique phrase about making a blessing, gives two constructions of the promise and corrects the text to my hand; Keil and Delitzsch read the clause about coming out as a demand for surrender.

debates.question: What does the offer actually promise?

sides.position: A return to their farms until the Egyptian campaign closes, after which they will be moved to an equal home
holders: Cheyne, as reported by Charles Ellicott

sides.position: That immediate surrender brings no harm, and they shall enjoy their own land until removed to a better
Nothing: the free use lasts just as long as the conqueror pleases, and a land like their own holds nothing they may call their own

outliers.note: He alone answers the offer with a proverb, that gilding the chain is enough to make the vulgar let you bind them.

themes: until I come and take you away
29.pericope_label: Let not Hezekiah deceive you; make an agreement with me

schools.summary: Clarke states the reasoning and calls the blasphemy of the speech without parallel, admiring that Hezekiah referred the affront to the Lord whose it was.
Ellicott admits the inconsistency with the earlier claim and supplies the history of the cities named, while Keil and Delitzsch state the conclusion the argument drives at.

sides.position: Place-names, since Ava and the Avites occur elsewhere and the versions support it
One word, an epithet of the city before them meaning the utterly perverted
holders: Hoffmann, as reported by Charles Ellicott

sides.position: Two Hebrew verbs, so that the clause is a question about who made them wander
holders: the Targum, as reported by Charles Ellicott

outliers.note: He alone grants that the speech contradicts itself, and excuses it by the occasion, since a man extemporising to frighten his hearers would not be particular about consistency.

themes: that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem
33.pericope_label: Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land?

schools.summary: Henry insists the silence was not for want of an answer, lists what might justly have been said, and reads the rent clothes as grief for Jerusalem as well as detestation of blasphemy.
Clarke explains the custom of rending garments at blasphemy and traces the chain by which the matter reached God.
Keil and Delitzsch find two purposes in the order of silence, and read the gesture as grief at words blaspheming Jehovah more than the king.

debates.question: Why were the people ordered not to answer?

sides.position: To stop him saying more, and to leave the ambassadors uncertain what impression they had made
Because the blasphemy was too barefaced to argue with, the quarrel being Jehovah's to avenge
Because there are men to whom offering anything religious or rational is casting pearls before swine

outliers.note: He alone traces the sequence of mediation, from ambassadors to the king as God's representative, to the prophet as God's minister, to God through the people's mediator.

themes: what might justly have been said
36.pericope_label: The people held their peace; Eliakim and Shebna came with clothes rent
